data.name: Gold Rush In The Oort Cloud
data.detailed_description:
Greetings!
Welcome to the SSGMC - Solar System Gold Mining Corp.
Now you're part of our family - colony 26168.
Your name is - Prisoner N57691.
Your task - participation in correctional work in the Oort cloud.
You're going to mine a gold! Gold from asteroids.
You will be given a spacesuit and a gun, but do not try to violate regime.
You will be sent into space without a spacesuit. And without a gun.
There is a lot of pirates in each region.
You have to destroy them all before you can return.
For this work you will get the money. Some of them you can spend on improving your equipment.
After release, you can spend it on alcohol and whores, as you wish.
We will give you a room on the space station with good views of the Neptune.
Work hard and you do not even notice how fast time will slip away!

reviews.review:
Gold Rush In The Oort Cloud is a compact indie action game that combines asteroid mining, shooting, platforming, and dark comedy within an intentionally bleak science-fiction setting. Developed and published by WTFOMGames, the game puts the player in the role of Prisoner N57691, a convict assigned to correctional labor for the Solar System Gold Mining Corp. Instead of presenting space exploration as a heroic journey into the unknown, the premise turns it into a dangerous corporate work assignment where survival and productivity are essentially the same thing.

The setup is easily one of the game's most distinctive qualities. The player belongs to colony 26168 and is ordered into the Oort Cloud to extract gold from asteroids. A spacesuit and firearm are provided, but these are presented as privileges that can quickly disappear if the prisoner refuses to cooperate. The corporation's threatening attitude establishes a dystopian atmosphere while also serving as the foundation for the game's deliberately crude humor. The contrast between cheerful corporate language and the brutal reality of forced labor gives the setting an amusingly cynical personality.

Gameplay focuses primarily on action rather than realistic mining simulation. Each region contains hostile pirates that must be eliminated before the player is allowed to return. This gives exploration a clear combat objective while asteroid mining provides the economic motivation for entering dangerous territory. The combination of shooting, movement, resource gathering, and enemy encounters creates a simple arcade-oriented gameplay loop. Players expecting a sophisticated industrial simulation should adjust their expectations, because mining is incorporated into an action game rather than developed into a complicated economic system.

Money earned from completing the prisoner's work can be spent on equipment improvements. This progression system adds some purpose to repeated excursions because better equipment makes the character increasingly capable of handling the dangers encountered in space. It also fits the dystopian premise particularly well. The prisoner is effectively paid for risking their life and then encouraged to spend those earnings on equipment that allows them to continue performing the same hazardous job. It is a straightforward progression concept, but it works naturally within the game's corporate satire.

The Oort Cloud setting provides an appealing backdrop for such a small production. Space naturally creates a feeling of isolation, and the idea of being stranded far from civilization while working for an uncaring corporation reinforces that loneliness. Even the promise of accommodation on a station overlooking Neptune carries an amusingly depressing undertone. The supposedly attractive view is presented as a workplace benefit while the protagonist remains trapped in an exploitative correctional system. These little details give the game more personality than its simple mechanics might initially suggest.

Its humor is intentionally rough and will probably be one of the most divisive aspects of the experience. The writing uses dark comedy, exaggerated threats, and crude adult jokes rather than subtle satire. There is a certain charm to how unapologetically ridiculous the corporation sounds, particularly when it refers to prisoners as members of its family while casually threatening them with death in space. However, players who dislike vulgar or deliberately tasteless comedy may find the writing more irritating than amusing. The humor should therefore be viewed as part of the game's niche identity rather than a universally appealing feature.

The overall mechanical scope remains fairly limited. Although the Steam tags cover action, platforming, shooting, mining, bullet hell, management, adventure, and science fiction, the game should not be mistaken for an expansive combination of all those genres. Its ideas are presented on a much smaller scale. The primary attraction is the mixture of arcade combat and mining within a quirky setting rather than deep systems, extensive exploration, or elaborate storytelling. Players who enjoy obscure indie titles may appreciate this directness, while those expecting a large space sandbox are likely to find it too basic.

Presentation follows the same modest philosophy. The futuristic environment and asteroid-mining concept provide enough visual context to support the gameplay, but spectacle is not the main attraction. Much of the experience depends on whether the player enjoys its unconventional premise and uncomplicated action. The game is single-player and supports an English interface, making it a particularly straightforward experience without multiplayer systems or extensive additional modes competing for attention.

Steam Deck compatibility is currently uncertain. The Steam store does not provide a confirmed Steam Deck Verified or Playable rating for the game, and reliable compatibility information is limited. It is therefore best treated as officially unverified for Steam Deck rather than assumed to work perfectly. Its relatively lightweight technical requirements may appear encouraging, but that alone does not guarantee proper controls, display behavior, or compatibility through SteamOS and Proton.

Gold Rush In The Oort Cloud ultimately succeeds more as a strange indie curiosity than as a deep space-mining adventure. Its strongest qualities are the absurd correctional-labor premise, dystopian corporate humor, and uncomplicated combination of asteroid mining and pirate combat. The progression system gives the action some direction, while the setting prevents the basic mechanics from feeling completely generic. Its weaknesses come primarily from its narrow scope, limited depth, rough presentation, and comedy that will not appeal to everyone. For players interested in unusual low-budget science-fiction games and straightforward arcade action, there is some entertainment to be found in its bizarre vision of employment at the edge of the solar system.

Rating: 4/10
